questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: English language courses, access to faculties other than my own course of study, university-assisted housing

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UCC did wonderful in making my Erasmus stay as smooth and easy as possible, although I do think that their claim to "assist with housing" is false. They do not provide housing or any guarantee of housing, they provide *help* with *finding* housing, which I found to be very different. I think mainly the unexpected housing crisis in Ireland might have something to do with this, and it definitely influenced my stay and experience in general, because I ended up in a shitty room with shared bathroom and kitchen, paying double what I'd do in Copenhagen for my own studio apartment, fully renovated, complete bath and kitchen.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Easy! UCC is good at communication and really spelling things out for everyone.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't need any extraordinary assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: None

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It wasn't easy, everything was booked when I started searching after I found out the university does in fact *not* provide housing to Erasmus students. Also, I couldn't have started applaying any earlier, because we didn't have our student login and whatnot. But I used a Cork Erasmus facebook group and they had a whole list of private and university-owned accommodation, which I emailed one by one in hopes of a room.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Don't live too far! the buses are *so* unrealiable, it's like they don't exist. And biking felt very unsafe because there were no bike lanes and the roads are narrow and pedestrians would walk all over the place because they're not used to looking out for cyclists. Also, my bike was super expensive in the end so I'm not sure I'd recommend getting one at all. You can walk, at least from where I lived (Brookfield).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: No housing guaranteed :) It was basically a lottery which every UCC visiting student entered. Some unis from the US had some sort of agreement with UCC, but I guess not UCPH.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Easy, they have a portal for all that. It was tough navigating the time schedules but you got used to it pretty quick. And they allowed for changes pretty late into the year!

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: They have a portal exclusively for Visiting Students so that nothing can go wrong. The application process in itself and selection of courses was so easy, but the approval took a long time to get. I was rejected from one class but I emailed my professor and got in anyway, so they're really flexible.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The International Office, the Administrative Office and your lecturers and professors.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got everything I wanted in the end

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
All courses are pretty small and superficial, the largest ECTS they had was 10 credits, which means you have between 3-6 courses total (most are 5 ECTS). There was barely any reading (except for my literature course, understandably), most of it was recommended which took me some time to adjust to, and they announce clearly (through canvas) when texts are required for class. 
At KU I have 2 x 15 ECTS courses. At UCC I had a total of 4 courses, which was perfect! They never went that deep into the subjects because their are weighted so lightly, so I took that as a chance to try out something different from the usual English department (music theory, film history, coding) and I think that was a good choice because they weren't that hard bc courses are so small and superficial. But during exam season some student with 5-6 courses were so overwhelmed, and I was glad I'd prioritized courses with portfolio or even an oral exam at the end, so I only had to write 2 essays of 1500 and 3000 words. So easy! Their essay length is so short even during exams that it wasn't that bad, having more work throughout the year compared to KU's 16-20 pages final assignments.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Lots of courses to choose from! Since you're in 3-6 classes they risk overlapping so that does limit things but in the end I did *not* end up with classes that I was uninterested in, and that is a win for me <3

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I wanted a year of rest and relaxation and lots of pints, and the academic term as UCC allowed that :) not to be mean but they didn't really go into any depth, and because the assignments are so limited in length you're barely able to quote from secondary sources without running out of space. Also, thier grading is kind of weird, as in, they rarely grade above 75 or below 60 (as far as I understood) so you can't really flunk, I guess. I turned in some rather shallow analyses but still got 75. I even heard that in some of the first year courses professors would ask the class to do 500 word assignments on "what does 'baroque' mean to you" or something lmao

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The professors would ask the class questions and students would answer but it would never really be a class discussion, it was more so an interactive lecture I suppose. Not that I minded but it was a little unstimulating and most questions and their answers were so surface-level lol, the discourse around texts and class material was really based in "I feel like" and "I think this". Lots of opinions backed by no critical approach and that pissed me off lol but at least it was easy and approachable, I learnt quickly to not be intimidated by the Irish students and how to assess the level of the class etc.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introduction to Irish Literature (10 ECTS)
Music Theory and Aural Skills (5 ECTS)
Case Studies in European Cinema (5 ECTS)
American Cinema 1953-73 (10 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I was satisfied with all of them!
The best was European Cinema, the movies were great and there weren't too many, the following classes on them were super interesting and engaging and easy to follow while still containing lots of information. And the exam was a 20-minute oral exam where, I gotta say, I've never had to fight harder to get a word in and to raise the taxonimical level lmao they really just asked "what did you think of this one, did you like it, do you think it is relevant today" etc. But easy and that's how I like it >:)
Intro to Irish was really good and the professor was great at engaging the class so I didn't even mind the 17-18 lecture on a Thursday (and when I did, I didn't show up, and he uploaded the lectures to canvas the day after)
American Cinema was also really good but there were far more movies to watch which would get a little stressful, and some of them I thought we could have skipped because the material and discussion overlapped. But Gwenda Young was an amazing and very knowledgable professor, I loved listening to her takes and general approach to film, she was great.
Music Theory and Aural Skills was basic music theory and sightsinging, BUT if you don't play and instrument or can't read sheet music or have never done formal education in music I'd say it was too hard, simply because the teacher would assume we all understood the material because most students had Music as their majors and therefore knew everything beforehand. The stuff was rather easy but she'd just skip explaining everything and it would go by really fast. But other than that, it was the easiest 5 ECTS of my life.

Housing DKK per month *

Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I bought a bike and made a deal with the seller that he'd buy it back at the end of the term. I thought he said "30-40% off of the original price" so that I'd be getting 70% back after 4 months use, but he really said "30-40% *of* the original price" so that was a shock to me, that after four months I had basically rented a crappy bike that was barely my size for what you could buy a new ladies city bike complete with everything back home. That sucked. But in the end I'm glad I had it since the buses barely showed up and the ones I knew who lived out of town or didn't own a bike basically spent the same or more on taxis to get around.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: A pint was 6€???? A normal, standard, low-priced pint was 6€!! so the first 10 days I was there I'd spent 500 DKK on beer alone lol that was excessive and I was very surprised that beer of all things in Ireland was going to be so expensive. Barista coffee, however, a flat white or cappucino was around 3-4€ so I ended up drinking less beer and more coffee, completely opposite to what I'd predicted about going to Ireland

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: So many clubs and societies! I joined all that I wanted but didn't really use them that much or to the extent that I expected but they were nice to have a the beginning to meet people, although mostly first years showed up (18-year-olds who still live at home)

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I loved the English Lit society, they did Twilight screenings and book speeddating and those were the best society events in my opinion, great ways to meet likeminded people who are very different from you.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: We rented an airbnb in the mountains of Kerry and that was hands down the peak of my Erasmus semester even if it was only for a weekend. Stunning nature, stunning views, small roads and lots of sheep, exactly what I'd expected to see in Ireland (something that the city of Cork, unfortunately, did not deliver)

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Drink beer, go to the movies, visit cafés, go on walks, go to concerts or shows, Crane Lane Theatre, the café at 107 Barrack Street owned by an old couple who sell vintage items and fun little knicknacks

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Ireland is very much like Denmark in its general behavior, but I will say the lack of infrastructural development was staggering. The roads were so badly kept, the house facades even at the center of town were rundown and deteriorating, they still had satellite TV everywhere and the phonelines were a mess attached to wooden poles along the sidewalk. And the public transportation! It sucked! It barely existed!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I'd say go out on Thursdays, that's when all the students go out because they go home to their parents' on the weekends, surely you'll meet someone there. Also, don't be afraid to talk to someone after class, pretend you have a question lol they're so naturally talkative, I found everyone really easy going (if a little young — third years are like 20)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Everyone goes clubbing lmao thank God for the older friends I made that were way past that phase otherwise I don't think I'd go out as much as I did

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openminded friendlyness, Ireland I think has a natural interest towards people from other countries  (at least towards mine lol) so they'd be really eager to ask what language we were speaking if we were in a group of Danes and that would start the conversation.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be prepared to pay double if not triple your usual rent
2. for the love of God get accommodation with walking distance to campus and to town — you cannot rely on public transit
3. Drink Beamish

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not that I can think of

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know people — I coordinated my semester with two others Danish people I met because we were all going to Cork and being able to share the experience (ups as well as downs) with someone *and* being able to bring those friendships back with me, I think, is the best part. A lot of people expect to get close to locals or to other exchange students, but I will say, don't hesitate to invest in the Danish people, too, even if it is rather stigmatized to go to a foreign country and just hang out with your own locals. Ignore that thought, lower your expectation of hanging out with mainly Irish people because it's not gonna happen and you'll be fine.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding housing that filled my needs but also was affordable and also had good location was difficult especially because I did not want to bet on finding something when I arrived. The entire administrative process pre-arrival also wasn't easy and demanded a lot of my own attention and independent research as info wasn't given out by KU for some reason, so a lot of emails and a lot of person-to-person communication rather than filling out forms with available information.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: None

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
